page.text:
Above we discussed how a specification has an associated statement form,
but you can also create statements explicitly using the `States:`
construct.

For example, the following communciates the statement that $x$ is not an
element of a set $X$.

```mlg
[x \.not.in./ X]
States:
when: x, X is \set
that:
. not: x "in"? X
Documented:
. written: "x? \notin X?"
Id: "756e0f48-1c0e-4e05-b97a-9c4fcd577603"
```

The `<arg> \. ... ./ <arg>` syntax is used to specify a statement and
here we specify what the statement means in the `that:` section.

Again note that statements do *not* introduce new symbols but instead
make statements about existing symbols.

Thus one **cannot** write:
```mlg-fragment
exists: x \.not.in./ X
suchThat: ...
```

but one could write:
```mlg-fragment
exists: x is \set
suchThat: x \.not.in./ X
```
That is, `x` needs to first be introduced and then a statement about it
can be expressed.

With the `States:` construct we can write more compact forms of
statements. For example, consider the following:

```mlg
[P \.iff./ Q]
States:
when: P, Q is \\statement
that:
. have: P
  iff: Q
Documented:
. written: "P? \iff Q?"
Id: "e0ad7367-d31b-433a-8a9c-c631d59a2632"
```

Here we made a shorthand for expressing a statement `P` is true if and
only if a statement `Q` is true. The builtin `\\statement` is the type of
statements.

With the above, one could write `(x "in"? X) \.iff./ (x "in"? Y)` for
example.

Note that the signature of a `States:` doesn't have to be of the form
`<arg> \. ... ./ <arg>`. For example consider the following,

```mlg
[\if{P}:then{Q}]
States:
when: P, Q is \\statement
that:
. if: P
  then: Q
Documented:
. written: "P? \Rightarrow Q?"
Id: "e1d413e6-767b-4b1f-a77c-64a169fb70d3"
```
which represents if `P` implies `Q`.

All of the above statements are included below:
